title: Within-Ancestry Testing vs Meta-Analysis
subtitle: A significant summary is not the same biology everywhere
learningObjectives: Distinguish within-ancestry estimates from fixed-effect and random-effects summaries.
Read the weight each ancestry group receives, and explain why the fixed-effect summary ignores heterogeneity.
Decide when a combined estimate is a fair biological claim for every group it combines.

prediction.question: Four ancestry groups are meta-analysed. Push heterogeneity to 100%, where the East Asian effect is about 3 times the others'. What happens to the fixed-effect summary?

options.label: Its interval widens like the random-effects one

interpretation.prompt: Does a significant meta-analysis mean the same biology is operating in every ancestry group?
interpretation.whatChanged: The fixed-effect summary stays narrow and significant at every level of heterogeneity because its weights never change: they are set by precision alone, so the two largest groups carry about three quarters of the weight and the East Asian group, where the effect is about 3 times larger, carries about a seventh. The random-effects model lets tau² re-balance the weights toward equality and its interval widens to say so. Only within-ancestry testing reports the East Asian effect itself.
interpretation.whyItMatters: A meta-analysis summary describes the groups that carry its weight. When the distinctive biology sits in a small group, the combined p-value can be impressive while saying nothing about that group; equity-aware synthesis reports the weights, the heterogeneity, and the within-ancestry estimates, not only the strongest combined p-value.
interpretation.facilitatorNote: Switch the synthesis select through its three settings before touching the slider: within-ancestry reports four estimates and four p-values; each meta-analysis reports one diamond, one p-value, and prints the weight each group carried on its row. Then set heterogeneity to 0: the two summaries coincide and I² is near zero. Move to 100. The fixed-effect weights do not move, the summary stays narrow and significant, and the rows show why: the East Asian group with the 3-fold effect carries about 15% of the weight. This is the meta-analysis half of the Sirugo quote on the framing slides (diverse populations 'only as part of large meta-analyses'), and it is also what Tractor-style local-ancestry analysis does after stratifying (module 3).

discussionPrompts: Would you report this as one shared effect, heterogeneous evidence, or both?
Which group needs more data before a biology claim is fair, and would more data change its weight?

alleleFrequencies.note: ADH1B Arg48His. Common in East Asian ancestry and rare elsewhere, so a multi-ancestry meta-analysis averages over groups that carry very different amounts of information about the variant.

realInputs.ancestryDistribution: All of Us Research Program, genomic data release v7 (~245,000 short-read whole genomes); ancestry proportions rounded to whole percent.

syntheticInputs: Group-specific effect sizes at full heterogeneity (0.05 / 0.06 / 0.22 / 0.08) are chosen to produce a realistic spread of I²; they are not published ADH1B effect estimates.
The heterogeneity slider linearly interpolates each group's effect between the common mean and its dispersed value.
assumptions: Additive dosage model, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, continuous phenotype standardised to unit variance.

Fixed-effect meta-analysis is inverse-variance weighted; random-effects uses the DerSimonian-Laird estimator of tau². The forest plot prints each group's share of 1/se² (fixed) or of 1/(se² + tau²) (random) under the selected summary.
provenance.derived: Standard errors, p-values, power, meta-analysis summaries, and heterogeneity statistics are computed from the inputs above by analysis/genetics.py; none are hand-entered.
